title: Thread pools and producer-consumer
idea: A thread pool reuses a fixed set of worker threads fed by a task queue. Producer-consumer splits making work from doing it through a blocking queue.
points: Creating a thread per task exhausts memory under load; a pool caps concurrent threads.
A bounded queue plus a rejection policy turns overload into a clear, early error.
`BlockingQueue.put` waits when full and `take` waits when empty: built-in backpressure.
Always `shutdown` then `awaitTermination`; a forgotten pool keeps the JVM alive.

hero.title: A producer fills a bounded queue

steps.caption: Three workers start and call `take`. The queue is empty, so all three block without using CPU.
The producer puts jobs 1 to 4. The queue now holds four jobs.
Waiting workers wake and each takes one job from the head of the queue.
The producer is faster and fills the queue again. Its next `put` blocks: that is backpressure.
Worker 1 finishes and takes j4. A slot frees up, so the producer's blocked put of j8 completes.
Workers drain j5 to j8. With no work left, the producer puts one poison pill per worker.
All workers have returned. `awaitTermination` now succeeds and the totals are final.

code.title: Bounded pool rejects overload
code.caption: Two workers and two queue slots. A latch keeps workers busy, so the fifth job finds the pool full.

walk.text: Build the pool yourself: fixed threads, a bounded queue, and an explicit rejection policy.
Each job is a `Callable`; `submit` returns a `Future` for its result.
Jobs 1 and 2 go straight to new workers; 3 and 4 wait in the queue.
Job 5 has no worker and no slot, so `AbortPolicy` throws instead of growing memory.
`Future.get` waits for each result, so they come back in submit order.
`shutdown` refuses new jobs; `awaitTermination` waits for running ones to finish.

code.title: Producer-consumer queue
code.caption: One producer and three consumers share a queue of four slots. Every job is handled exactly once.

walk.text: A 4-slot queue makes the producer wait. The pool has one extra thread: the producer is a task.
`put` blocks while full. After 20 jobs it sends one poison pill per consumer.
`take` blocks while empty. Each job goes to exactly one consumer.
On the poison pill the consumer returns, so its pool thread becomes free.
Restore the interrupt flag rather than swallow it, so the pool can stop the thread.
Wait for termination, then print totals that do not depend on which thread ran what.

pitfalls: `Executors.newFixedThreadPool` uses an unbounded queue: a slow consumer grows memory until it fails.
Sending one poison pill for three consumers: two consumers block forever and the pool never ends.
Ignoring the `Future` from `submit`: a task's exception is stored there and silently lost.

quiz.q: Pool: 2 threads, a queue of 2, `AbortPolicy`. Six jobs that block are submitted. What happens?
options: All six run; the pool adds threads
Four accepted; jobs 5 and 6 throw a rejection
Two accepted; the rest throw a rejection
The fifth `submit` call blocks until a slot frees
quiz.why: Two jobs occupy the workers and two fill the queue. With the maximum size reached, `AbortPolicy` throws `RejectedExecutionException` for each further job.

takeaway: Bound the threads, bound the queue, and decide what happens when both are full.

starters: How do I choose the pool size for CPU-bound vs I/O-bound work?
When should I use CallerRunsPolicy instead of AbortPolicy?
Is a poison pill better than interrupting the consumers?
